topic: Binomial Distributions: The Math of Success and Failure
target_audience: High school or introductory college students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
lecture_lines: A Bernoulli trial has exactly two outcomes.
We label success as p and failure as q.
Each dive Pixel takes is one independent trial.
animations: Show a central toggle switch labeled 'Trial' moving between 'Success' (#00FF00) and 'Failure' (#FF0000).
Display 'p' next to Success and 'q' next to Failure with light blue labels (#ADD8E6).
Show a cartoon penguin (Pixel) diving; a green check mark appears for success and a red X for failure.

sections.title: Defining the Binomial Distribution
lecture_lines: In a binomial distribution, we repeat several trials.
We count the probability of exactly k successes.
Tree diagrams show how possible outcomes branch out.
animations: Transform the single toggle into a row of 5 slots labeled 'n=5'.
Highlight 3 slots with 'Success' labels (#00FF00) and 2 with 'Failure' (#FF0000), showing 'k=3'.
Animate a branching tree starting from a single point, splitting into 'S' and 'F' paths for 3 levels.

sections.title: The 'BINS' Checklist
lecture_lines: Use the BINS acronym to check for binomial distributions.
B stands for Binary: outcomes are success or failure.
I means trials are independent of each other.
N requires a fixed number of trials.
S means the probability remains the same every time.
animations: Large letters 'BINS' appear in the center in bright cyan (#00FFFF).
Highlight 'B' (Binary) and show the Success/Failure toggle from Section 1.
Highlight 'I' (Independent) and show two dice rolling independently.
Highlight 'N' (Number) and show a counter hitting a fixed limit 'n=5'.
Highlight 'S' (Same p) and show a probability value fixed at 0.6.

sections.title: Visualizing the Formula
lecture_lines: This formula calculates the probability of specific outcomes.
nCk counts the different ways successes can occur.
p to the k is the probability of successes.
q to the n minus k covers the failures.
Combine these building blocks to find the total probability.
animations: Display the formula P(X=k) = nCk * p^k * q^(n-k) in large white font.
Highlight 'nCk' in yellow (#FFFF00) and show 5 slots rearranging 3 successes.
Highlight 'p^k' in green (#00FF00) and show the text 'p * p * p'.
Highlight 'q^(n-k)' in red (#FF0000) and show the text 'q * q'.
All three highlighted formula parts slide together to form the complete equation.

sections.title: The Shape of Probability
lecture_lines: Histograms visualize the probability of each success count.
Changing the probability p shifts the distribution's center.
Increasing the trial count n creates a bell shape.
animations: Draw a histogram with bars of varying heights on a simple x-y axis in light grey (#D3D3D3).
Animate the bars shifting right as a 'p' value slider moves from 0.1 to 0.9.
Increase the number of bars (n) from 5 to 20 and show the distribution smoothing into a bell curve.

sections.title: Real-World Application & Summary
lecture_lines: Binomial distributions help predict real-world manufacturing defects.
They allow factories to plan for expected failure rates.
Remember the BINS criteria for any binomial problem.
animations: Show a conveyor belt with a robot scanning items; highlight 'Pass' (#00FF00) and 'Fail' (#FF0000).
Display a digital factory report showing a predicted defect rate calculation.
Flash the BINS acronym one last time in a golden color (#FFD700).
